newsitem.title: GERMANY: Berlin remembers Wall murders on 36th anniversary.
newsitem.headline: Berlin remembers Wall murders on 36th anniversary.

text.p: Berlin solemnly marked the 36th anniversary of the building of the Berlin Wall on Wednesday by honouring the victim of one of the most grisly killings in its no-man's land.
Berlin politicians laid wreaths at the spot near Allied border crossing Checkpoint Charlie where 18-year-old mason Peter Fechter was shot in August 1962 and bled to death.

Berlin Mayor Eberhard Diepgen quietly placed a ring of roses at the large wooden cross marking the site and blamed the hated division of Germany for the deaths of many would-be dissidents along the guarded borders between east and west.

"The Berlin Wall is history, thank God," Diepgen said. "But it and its victims have not been forgotten. It defined German and European history for decades and served as a symbol of the division of the continent."
Evidence gathered by the independent August 13 Working Group suggests at least 916 people were killed trying to escape from the former communist East Germany, 265 on the Wall itself.

Chancellor Helmut Kohl on Tuesday said the anniversary of the building of the 155-km (96-mile) cement and barbed wire barrier was a reminder of the need to remain vigilant in fighting extremism and defending democracy.

Unified Germany has attempted to bring to book those behind the deaths on the border since the Wall fell in 1989, but courts have refrained from giving hefty sentences to former border guards who have claimed they were carrying out orders.
Egon Krenz, the last hardline East German leader, and three of his deputies are currently on trial accused of giving shoot-to-kill orders on the border. A verdict is expected in coming weeks.
A Berlin court in March convicted two former East German border guards of manslaughter for the Fechter shooting and sentenced them to 20 and 21 months probation.
Fechter lay bleeding for 50 minutes while East German border guards ignored his screams and Western Allies tried in vain to help by tossing bandages over the Wall.

East German police finally carried away his limp body and he later died in hospital. Fechter's case was unique for its cruelty and brought the brutality of the communist regime to light in horrifying pictures published around the world.
The otherwise sombre ceremony was disrupted by shouting matches between East Berliners and members of the Party of Democratic Socialism (PDS), the successor to East Germany's Communist Party.

The PDS brings a wreath of its own every year to lay at the foot of the cross, an act which enrages the Wall's victims, some of whom arrived in wheelchairs due to injuries they suffered trying to escape to the West.
"Every year it just seems to get more brazen," said Klaus-Peter Eich, who said he was shot by East German border guards in 1961 and was left paralysed from the neck down.
"It is scandalous for the victims," Eich said. "It shows either deep cynicism or schizophrenia (on the part of the PDS)."

Several tourists passing by said the few fragments remaining of the Wall and the Fechter memorial were more vivid than any museum could be and remembered the day they heard the Wall had been erected on August 13, 1961.
"It was a shocking moment," said Frank Host, a pensioner from Chicago on holiday in Berlin. "It was almost inconceivable that a city could just be divided almost overnight."
